papers.title: Migrant scientists and international networks
papers.authors: Giuseppe Scellato; Chiara Franzoni; Paula Stephan
papers.research_question: Do foreign-born (migrant) scientists have more international research collaborations than non-migrants and returnees, and do they keep collaborating with their country of origin?
papers.data: GlobSci survey (2011) of scientists working in 16 countries, comparing foreign-born, native non-mobile, and returnee scientists. An earlier version is NBER WP 18613 (2012), 'Mobile Scientists and International Networks'.
papers.methods: Survey-based econometric comparison of collaboration patterns by migration status and by where the PhD was obtained.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: migrants are more likely to collaborate internationally, mainly those who did their PhD abroad and came to the destination for a postdoc or a job. A sizeable share of the foreign-born collaborate with researchers in their country of origin (a 'diaspora effect'). Migrants from a relatively stronger science base have superior networks to those from a weaker one.
papers.relevance_to_project: Individual-level micro-foundation for a migrant-to-origin co-authorship link. The result that network benefits depend on the origin's science base implies that for weak-science-base origins (many SSA focus countries) migrant destinations may not translate into collaboration partners, which is the mismatch hypothesis. Useful for interpreting PPML coefficients on migrant stocks by origin capacity.

papers.title: National ties of international scientific collaboration and researcher mobility found in Nature and Science
papers.authors: Maki Kato; Asao Ando
papers.research_question: Is country-level international scientific collaboration explained by researchers' international migration as well as by their motivation, and which way does causality run between mobility and collaboration?
papers.data: Metadata of papers published in Nature and Science, 1989-2009 (country-pair counts).
papers.methods: Count-data estimation on bilateral (country-pair) collaboration, with migration (mobility) variables and 'synergy' and 'difference' effects between countries. The direction of the mobility-collaboration relationship is tested.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: international collaboration is explained by both researchers' international migration and their motivation (synergy and difference effects between countries). Researchers move to countries with better research environments, but networks created through collaboration are not a factor in migration. The relationship runs in one direction, from mobility to collaboration. The paper also notes a mechanical issue: when a researcher moves from A to B, a former A-B collaboration becomes domestic and a tie to A becomes international.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest country-pair econometric precedent for using scholarly mobility to predict co-authorship (our component b). The mechanical reclassification point is directly relevant to our design, because Akbaritabar et al. mobility flows and OpenAlex co-authorship come from the same affiliation records, so the gravity models need lagging or disjoint author sets.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch: the IDEAS/RePEc record URL encodes DOI 10.1007/s11192-016-2183-z with the matching title, and a library catalogue record gives Scientometrics 2017, 110(2), pp. 673-694.

papers.title: Travel bans and scientific mobility: utility of asymmetry and affinity indexes to inform science policy
papers.authors: Zaida Chinchilla-Rodríguez; Yi Bu; Nicolás Robinson-García; Rodrigo Costas; Cassidy R. Sugimoto
papers.research_question: Can asymmetry and affinity indexes computed separately for scientific collaboration and scientific mobility reveal the strength of, and discrepancies between, bilateral research relationships, using the countries named in the 2017 US travel bans as a test case?
papers.data: Bibliometric collaboration and author-mobility data for the countries in the 2017 US executive-order travel bans (Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Yemen) and their partner countries.
papers.methods: Affinity Index (AFI) and Probabilistic Affinity Index (PAI, also called the Proximity Index) computed for collaboration and for mobility links, plus asymmetry indexes, with the two layers compared for each country.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: comparing collaboration and mobility from an affinity perspective can identify discrepancies between levels of collaboration and levels of mobility. The probabilistic affinity index is highly sensitive to country size. The authors argue that the approach can inform immigration policy and identify potential partnerships.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest precedent for component (a). For each origin (including Somalia, a focus origin) it compares the partner profile of one network layer (bibliometric mobility) against another (co-authorship) and flags mismatches. Our project extends this with UN DESA general migrant stocks as a third layer and with formal divergence metrics (JSD, rank correlation, top-k overlap) and null models instead of affinity indexes alone. Its finding on size sensitivity motivates our degree- and strength-preserving nulls.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch: the Springer DOI URL link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11192-018-2738-2 is listed with the matching title, along with the IDEAS record (v116y2018i1d10.1007_s11192-018-2738-2), IU ScholarWorks, and the open-access Leiden repository PDF.

papers.title: A Global Comparison of Scientific Mobility and Collaboration According to National Scientific Capacities
papers.authors: Zaida Chinchilla-Rodríguez; Lili Miao; Dakota Murray; Nicolás Robinson-García; Rodrigo Costas; Cassidy R. Sugimoto
papers.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics 3: 17
papers.research_question: How do country-level networks of scientific mobility and international collaboration relate to each other, and how does this vary with national scientific capacity?
papers.data: Bibliometric affiliation data, 2008-2015. Countries are linked when an individual is affiliated with both. National capacity comes from the Scientific and Technological Capacity Index (150 countries: 22 Advanced, 24 Proficient, 22 Developing, 80 Lagging).
papers.methods: Construction and comparison of country mobility and collaboration networks, stratified by capacity group, using network positions and centrality.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: there is a significant relationship between the flow of mobile researchers and co-publication with foreign partners in the more prolific countries, but mobility is always lower than collaboration. Relationships are size- and resource-dependent. Advanced and Proficient countries hold most mobile authors and international papers, and mobility is extremely low in Developing and Lagging countries. Country positions are not consistent across the two networks, which shows distinct roles for mobility and collaboration, with particular instability for lower-income countries.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest global, multilayer topology comparison of a mobility network and a collaboration network (our multilayer and topology component). Its finding that the layers diverge most for lower-income countries directly anticipates our SSA focus. It does not include general (UN DESA) migration and does not use null models, which are our additions.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch: the Frontiers PDF URL and doi.org/10.3389/frma.2018.00017 are listed with the matching title, and the summary gives the authors, volume 3, article 17, and publication on 23 May 2018.

papers.title: Analyzing scientific mobility and collaboration in the Middle East and North Africa
papers.authors: Jamal El Ouahi; Nicolás Robinson-García; Rodrigo Costas
papers.research_question: How do scientific mobility and international collaboration networks of MENA countries compare in structure and in partner affinity?
papers.data: Bibliometric publication and affiliation data for MENA countries, 2008-2017. A dataset is archived on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.5155979). The arXiv preprint is 2009.07815.
papers.methods: Country-level mobility and co-authorship networks, degree and affinity indicators, and comparison of the two layers.
papers.findings: Abstract-level from search snippets: international co-authorship is more frequent than international mobility. The mobility network is thinner than the collaboration network in terms of affinity between countries. The hubs differ: Saudi Arabia has the highest degree in mobility, while Turkey has the highest in collaboration.

Like the other CWTS/Sugimoto studies, it uses only scholarly mobility and no general migrant stocks.

papers.title: Studying scientific migration in Scopus
papers.authors: Henk F. Moed; M'hamed Aisati; Andrew Plume
papers.research_question: Can Scopus author profiles and affiliation linking be used to measure international scientific migration, and how do migration patterns relate to international co-authorship?
papers.data: Scopus author-affiliation histories for five countries (Germany, Italy, Netherlands, UK, USA), 1999-2010.
papers.methods: Bibliometric tracking of author affiliation changes, compared with co-authorship patterns between the same countries.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: language similarity between countries is a more important factor in international migration than in international co-authorship. Example balances are given (the Netherlands had a positive migration balance with the UK and a negative one with Germany). A secondary search summary attributes to the paper the result that having international co-authors increases the probability of international movement (not confirmed in full text).
papers.relevance_to_project: Early direct evidence that migration and co-authorship respond differently to the same dyadic factors (language), which supports treating them as distinct layers and expecting misalignment. Its scholarly-migration measure is the methodological ancestor of the Akbaritabar et al. (2024) flows we use.

papers.title: International Scientific Migration and Collaboration Patterns Following a Bibliometrics Line of Investigation
papers.authors: Gali Halevi; Henk F. Moed
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (CoRR abs/1212.5194). A related peer-reviewed paper is Moed & Halevi (2014), 'A bibliometric approach to tracking international scientific migration', Scientometrics 101(3): 1987-2001, DOI 10.1007/s11192-014-1307-6
papers.research_question: Can Scopus affiliation data track international scientific migration, and do migration patterns differ from co-authorship (collaboration) patterns between countries?
papers.data: Scopus affiliation countries of publishing authors for 17 countries (10 fast-growing and 7 established science systems).
papers.methods: Synchronous and asynchronous bibliometric migration indicators compared with country-level co-authorship patterns, with error-rate estimation.
papers.findings: Abstract-level and secondary coverage (Inside Higher Ed, Research Trends): international scientific migration patterns are different from collaboration patterns. Shared language and geographic proximity affect migration more strongly than co-authorship, and political tensions affect co-authorship more than migration. Results should be interpreted cautiously and combined with CV or survey data.
papers.relevance_to_project: The most direct early statement of our headline claim that the migration network is not the collaboration network, though here 'migration' means bibliometric scholarly mobility, not general population migrant stocks. We should cite it as a precursor and show that the divergence also holds, and is larger, when general migration (UN DESA) is the comparison layer.

papers.title: Highly skilled migration and the internationalization of knowledge
papers.authors: Claudia Noumedem Temgoua
papers.venue: Cahiers du GREThA (Université de Bordeaux) Working Paper n° 2018-16
papers.research_question: Do Chinese and Indian highly skilled diasporas foster international knowledge networks (co-authorship and co-inventorship) among OECD destination countries?
papers.data: OECD destination-country pairs, with bilateral co-authorship (publications) and co-inventorship (patents) and highly skilled diaspora stocks by origin (China, India; also Vietnam, Pakistan, Iran).
papers.methods: Gravity model at the country-pair level. The search summary of the working paper text describes PPML estimation with co-authorship and co-inventorship as dependent variables, controlling for other migration variables.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: OECD country pairs hosting sizeable portions of the Indian or Chinese highly skilled diaspora collaborate more on publications and patents, after controlling for other migration variables. Smaller diasporas (Vietnam, Pakistan, Iran) produce similar effects on co-authorship and co-inventorship.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest precedent found for component (b): a PPML gravity model of bilateral co-authorship that separates a skilled-diaspora variable from other migration controls. Its dyads are destination-destination pairs linked by a shared third-country diaspora, whereas ours are origin-destination pairs with SSA origins, and it does not use bibliometric scholarly mobility. Journal publication status is unknown.

papers.title: Inventor Diasporas and the Internationalization of Technology
papers.authors: Ernest Miguélez
papers.research_question: Do diasporas of highly skilled (inventor) migrants increase cross-country inventive collaboration (co-patenting) and R&D offshoring between their host and origin countries?
papers.data: PCT patent applications. Inventors with a migrant background are used as a proxy for the skilled diaspora in each country pair.
papers.methods: Gravity models of bilateral international co-patenting (inventor-inventor co-inventorship and applicant-inventor links). Earlier versions are GREThA WP 2014-12 and World Bank Policy Research WP 7619.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: inventor diasporas are strongly and robustly associated with international co-patenting, and the effect shrinks as interactions become more formal (stronger for inventor-inventor co-inventorship than for applicant-inventor offshoring). The Chinese and Indian diasporas do not drive the results. The working-paper version reports that a 10% larger inventor diaspora is associated with 1.5-2.2% more international patent collaborations (not confirmed in the published version).
papers.relevance_to_project: The methodological template for including a skilled-diaspora stock in a PPML gravity model of bilateral knowledge collaboration. It is the patent analogue of our co-authorship model, and its contrast between skilled diaspora and general migration parallels our comparison of scholarly mobility with UN DESA migrant stocks.

papers.title: Which factors influence the international mobility of research scientists?
papers.authors: Silvia Appelt; Brigitte van Beuzekom; Fernando Galindo-Rueda; Roberto de Pinho
papers.venue: OECD Science, Technology and Industry Working Papers 2015/02. Also a chapter in Geuna (ed.), Global Mobility of Research Scientists (Academic Press, 2015), pp. 177-213
papers.research_question: What bilateral factors explain international flows of research scientists between countries?
papers.data: Bilateral scientist mobility measured from changes in affiliations reported by publishing scientists in a major global index of scholarly publications, 1996-2011.
papers.methods: Gravity model of bilateral scientist flows, with geographic, socioeconomic and scientific distance, co-authorship (collaboration) intensity, tertiary student flows, R&D resources and visa restrictions as regressors.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: geographic, socioeconomic and scientific distance correlate negatively with scientist mobility between two countries. Scientific collaboration is a major factor associated with mobility. Scientist mobility relies heavily on tertiary student flows in the opposite direction (destination to origin). Mobility is positively related to economic convergence and R&D resources, and negatively to visa restrictions.
papers.relevance_to_project: The reverse-direction counterpart to our component (b). It shows that bibliometric scholarly mobility and co-authorship are tightly coupled at the dyad level, so mobility is partly endogenous to collaboration. This supports lagged specifications and comparing the explanatory power of general migration (more exogenous to science) with scholarly mobility.
papers.verification_source: No DOI seen. Title, authors and the OECD STI WP 2015/2 series were confirmed via WebSearch (IDEAS/RePEc, EconBiz and OECD iLibrary pages).

papers.title: Quantifying the negative impact of brain drain on the integration of European science
papers.authors: Doria Arrieta (O. A.); Fabio Pammolli; Alexander M. Petersen
papers.research_question: Did EU enlargement (2004/2007) and the resulting high-skilled migration imbalance affect cross-border scientific collaboration and integration in Europe?
papers.data: Millions of publications for 32 European countries, 1996-2012, across 14 subject areas, plus official intra-European high-skilled mobility statistics.
papers.methods: Synthetic control method for the counterfactual level of cross-border collaboration, and difference-in-differences panel regressions relating collaboration to migration imbalance.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: European cross-border collaboration would have been higher absent the 2004/2007 enlargement. Migration imbalance, mostly from newer to older member states, is a major factor. The authors argue that this hampers convergence in scientific competitiveness and recommend home-return incentives.
papers.relevance_to_project: A quasi-causal, country-level study linking official (non-bibliometric) high-skilled migration to co-authorship. It shows that migration can coincide with weaker, not stronger, collaboration with the origin (brain drain rather than bridge), which our residual analysis for SSA origins can test.

papers.title: Collaborating with People Like Me: Ethnic Coauthorship within the United States
papers.authors: Richard B. Freeman; Wei Huang
papers.research_question: Do US-based scientists of the same ethnicity coauthor more than expected, and how does ethnic homophily relate to research impact?
papers.data: Authorship of scientific papers by US-based authors, with ethnicity inferred from names (IZA DP 8432 is an earlier version).
papers.methods: Comparison of observed ethnic co-authorship against the expectation from the ethnic composition of authors, and regressions of journal impact and citations on homophily.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: persons of similar ethnicity coauthor together more frequently than predicted by their share among authors. Greater homophily is associated with publication in lower-impact journals and with fewer citations.
papers.relevance_to_project: Evidence that shared ethnic or national origin structures co-authorship beyond chance, which is the mechanism behind expecting diaspora stocks to predict collaboration. Its observed-versus-expected logic is analogous to our residual and null-model approach. It is within-country, not cross-border, so it does not show that migrants link destination and origin.

papers.title: Bridging the Gap: Evidence from the Return Migration of African Scientists
papers.authors: Caroline Viola Fry
papers.research_question: Does the return migration of internationally trained African scientists raise the productivity and connections of non-migrant colleagues at the receiving African institutions?
papers.data: Return of US-trained African HIV/AIDS researchers supported by the NIH Fogarty program, with publication records of non-migrant scientists at the receiving African institutions.
papers.methods: Quasi-experimental design exploiting the timing of returnee arrivals at African institutions (difference-in-differences style comparison of exposed and unexposed non-migrants).
papers.findings: Abstract-level: non-migrant scientists at the receiving African institutions publish more after a returnee arrives, especially those without prior ties to top global institutions. Returnees act as brokers connecting peripheral colleagues to central knowledge and networks.
papers.relevance_to_project: The strongest causal evidence found for SSA that migration (via return) builds collaboration links between Africa and destination science systems. It suggests the migrant-collaboration link runs through a narrow, science-specific channel (trained researchers) rather than general diaspora size, which is the distinction our general-migration-versus-scholarly-mobility comparison tests.

papers.title: Migration and Global Network Formation: Evidence from Female Scientists in Developing Countries
papers.authors: Caroline Fry; Jeffrey L. Furman
papers.research_question: When do migrant scientists from developing countries broker international connections for non-migrant scientists at home, and how does institutional context (gender parity) shape this?
papers.data: PhD fellowship program of the Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World (OWSD), 1996-2016: female scientists from developing countries doing PhDs in another developing country. Panel of 3,179 non-migrant scientists in the published version.
papers.methods: Panel analysis of whether non-migrants gain international co-authorship connections through migrant colleagues, interacted with home- and host-country gender parity.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: female migrant scientists are more likely to share international connections with non-migrants at home when their home and host countries have high levels of gender parity. Institutional support is critical for migrant brokerage and the globalization of knowledge production.
papers.relevance_to_project: Developing-country evidence (including South-South migration) that migration translates into origin-country collaboration only under supportive institutional conditions. This gives a mechanism for heterogeneity across SSA origins in how well migrant destinations align with collaboration partners.

papers.title: From drains to bridges: The role of internationally mobile PhD students in linking non-mobile with foreign scientists
papers.authors: Rodrigo Ito; Diego Chavarro; Tommaso Ciarli; Robin Cowan; Fabiana Visentin
papers.research_question: Do internationally mobile PhD students and scientists from a developing country link non-mobile domestic scientists to foreign collaborators, and how durable are these links?
papers.data: CVs, scholarship program records and OpenAlex publications reconstructing the mobility paths and co-authorship networks of 19,158 Colombian scientists, 1990-2021. UNU-MERIT WP 2024-009 is an earlier version.

papers.title: Research upon return: The effect of international mobility on scientific ties, production and impact
papers.authors: Koen Jonkers; Laura Cruz-Castro
papers.research_question: How do ties formed during a stay in a foreign research system affect returnee scientists' international collaboration patterns, output and impact after return?
papers.data: Argentinean researchers who returned after working abroad, compared with non-mobile peers (bibliometric and CV data).
papers.methods: Econometric comparison of returnees' collaboration with former host countries and of their productivity and impact.
papers.findings: Abstract-level: highly skilled return migrants contribute to establishing ties between home and host research systems. Ties formed abroad shape returnees' collaboration patterns and research output upon return.
papers.relevance_to_project: Classic evidence that a country's collaboration partners mirror where its scientists went (former host countries), so scholarly mobility should predict collaboration better than general migrant destinations. This is a direct prior for our hypothesis on component (b).
papers.verification_source: WebSearch: a search-result snippet quotes 'Research Policy 42(8): 1366-1377. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2013.05.005' with the matching title, and the IDEAS and EconPapers records confirm the volume, issue and pages.

established: Migrant scientists have more international collaborations than non-migrants, and a sizeable share collaborate with their origin country (a 'diaspora effect'). Network benefits are larger for migrants from stronger science bases (Scellato, Franzoni & Stephan 2015).

At the country-pair level, researcher mobility predicts international collaboration, and the relationship runs from mobility to collaboration rather than the reverse. Mobility also mechanically reclassifies co-authorship as domestic or international (Kato & Ando 2017).

Scholarly mobility and co-authorship networks are correlated among prolific countries, but mobility is always sparser than collaboration. Country positions differ across the two layers, most of all for lower-income countries (Chinchilla-Rodríguez et al. 2018, Frontiers; El Ouahi, Robinson-García & Costas 2021 for MENA).

Affinity indexes computed separately for mobility and collaboration reveal bilateral discrepancies (mismatches), and the probabilistic affinity index is highly size-sensitive (Chinchilla-Rodríguez, Bu et al. 2018, travel-ban countries including Somalia).

Migration and co-authorship have different dyadic drivers: language similarity and geographic proximity matter more for migration, and political tensions matter more for collaboration (Moed, Aisati & Plume 2013; Halevi & Moed 2012).

Skilled diaspora stocks are associated with more bilateral knowledge collaboration in gravity models: co-authorship and co-invention for Chinese and Indian highly skilled diasporas net of other migration controls (Noumedem Temgoua 2018, working paper), and co-patenting for inventor diasporas, with the effect weakening for more formal links (Miguélez 2018).

Bilateral scientist mobility is strongly associated with co-authorship and with reverse-direction student flows in gravity models, so scholarly mobility is partly endogenous to collaboration (Appelt et al. 2015).

Migrants and returnees act as brokers who connect non-migrant colleagues at home to global networks, including in Sub-Saharan Africa: returning US-trained African HIV researchers raise non-migrant colleagues' output (Fry 2023). Brokerage depends on institutional context such as gender parity (Fry & Furman 2025). Mobile scientists link non-mobile Colombian peers to foreign collaborators, but those ties are short-lived without the mobile intermediary (Ito et al. 2025). Returnees maintain ties to former host systems (Jonkers & Cruz-Castro 2013; Jonkers & Tijssen 2008, Scientometrics 77(2), DOI 10.1007/s11192-007-1971-x).

Shared ethnicity raises co-authorship above chance (ethnic homophily), with lower-impact outcomes (Freeman & Huang 2015). Chinese diaspora researchers are over-represented in China's international collaborations (Xie & Freeman, NBER WP 27169, 2020/2021; not peer-reviewed; DOI not confirmed).

High-skilled migration imbalance can reduce cross-border collaboration with origin countries: EU enlargement and migration from new to old members lowered European scientific integration (Doria Arrieta, Pammolli & Petersen 2017).

Standard gravity determinants of country-pair co-authorship are geographic distance (negative), prior collaboration (positive) and common language (positive). This holds for Africa too, where past collaboration and shared language have the largest effects (Plotnikova & Rake 2014, Scientometrics 98(2), DOI 10.1007/s11192-013-1182-6; Cerdeira et al. 2023, Scientometrics 128, DOI 10.1007/s11192-023-04659-9). Neither abstract mentions migration as a regressor.
unresolved: No study was found that regresses bilateral co-authorship on UN DESA total (general-population) bilateral migrant stocks, or that compares general migrant stocks with bibliometric scholarly mobility (e.g. Akbaritabar, Theile & Zagheni 2024, Scientific Data, DOI 10.1038/s41597-024-03655-9) as competing predictors of co-authorship. This appears to be the gap our project fills, but the searches relied on WebSearch only and full texts were not read.

No study was found that computes per-origin divergence (JSD, top-k overlap or rank correlation with null models) between an origin's migrant-destination distribution and its collaboration-partner distribution. Existing work uses affinity indexes or centrality comparisons and scholarly mobility only.

Full-text verification was not possible because WebFetch was blocked: api.crossref.org and cahiersdugretha.u-bordeaux.fr failed to resolve and must be allowlisted in the session's network settings for direct Crossref or publisher checks. All DOI-title matches marked verified come from WebSearch result snippets or summaries (several from DOI-bearing URLs). Findings are abstract-level.

The country-specific results of the travel-ban paper for Somalia (and the other banned countries) were not retrieved. The full text (open access at Leiden's repository) should be checked for Somalia's mobility-versus-collaboration affinity mismatch, which is a direct comparison point for our Somalia results.

Noumedem Temgoua (2018): journal publication status, the exact migration controls (whether total bilateral stocks are included alongside skilled diaspora) and the exact estimator are unconfirmed. Its dyads are destination-destination pairs sharing a diaspora, not origin-destination pairs.

DOIs were not confirmed for Doria Arrieta et al. 2017 (Science Advances e1602232), Appelt et al. 2015 (OECD STI WP 2015/2), Xie & Freeman (NBER WP 27169) and Kahn & MacGarvie 2016 (Research Policy 45(6): 1304-1322, on Fulbright return requirements and home-country citations, with the strongest effects for low-income and weak-science countries). Kahn & MacGarvie's collaboration-specific results were not seen.

Evidence specific to the SSA scientific diaspora is thin. No bibliometric study was found that measures Ethiopian, Kenyan, Nigerian, Ghanaian, Ugandan, Tanzanian, Rwandan, Senegalese or Somali diaspora co-authorship with home institutions. Related evidence is Fry (2023) on returnees, Confraria, Swart & Blanckenberg (2020 book chapter; 2019 Sussex version), who find that African researchers with a foreign doctorate or recent mobility collaborate more with non-African researchers (no DOI confirmed), and program reports (e.g. the Carnegie African Diaspora Fellowship), which are not peer-reviewed evidence.

Shared-measurement endogeneity: the Akbaritabar et al. mobility flows and OpenAlex co-authorship are both derived from affiliation strings in the same bibliometric records. Kato & Ando (2017) note that a move mechanically turns a former international tie into a domestic one and vice versa. How prior work handled this, for example with disjoint author sets or lags, is unclear.

Baruffaldi & Landoni (2012), Research Policy 41(9): 1655-1665, DOI 10.1016/j.respol.2012.04.005 (verified via RePEc in WebSearch), was checked but left out of the list because of the 16-paper cap. It finds that home-country linkages raise both return probability and productivity abroad among 497 foreign researchers in Italy and Portugal. Ganguli (2015, JOLE 33(S1), DOI 10.1086/679741) and Kerr (2008, REStat 90(3), DOI 10.1162/rest.90.3.518) concern citations and patent diffusion rather than co-authorship, so they were excluded.

Pei et al. (2024), 'Co-evolution of international scientific mobility and international collaboration: a Scopus-based analysis', Scientometrics 129(7): 4353-4378 (the IDEAS URL encodes 10.1007/s11192-024-05081-5), reports increasingly interconnected global mobility and collaboration networks. Its methods were not reviewed, and it may be another close topology comparison.

A December 2025 arXiv preprint (Cai, Liu & Wang, 'How Visa-Free Policies Fuel International Research Collaboration: Evidence from China', arXiv 2512.12189) uses a staggered difference-in-differences design and reports that China's unilateral visa-free policy increased Sino-foreign co-authorship. It is not peer-reviewed and was not included.
sweep.closest_prior_work_to_our_contribution:
(a) Measuring the mismatch between an origin's migrant-destination distribution and its collaboration-partner distribution. The closest prior work is Chinchilla-Rodríguez, Bu, Robinson-García, Costas & Sugimoto (2018), 'Travel bans and scientific mobility: utility of asymmetry and affinity indexes to inform science policy', Scientometrics 116(1): 569-590, DOI 10.1007/s11192-018-2738-2. For the 2017 US travel-ban countries (Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Yemen), it computes affinity indexes separately for bibliometric mobility and for co-authorship and explicitly identifies discrepancies between the two. Its companion, Chinchilla-Rodríguez, Miao, Murray, Robinson-García, Costas & Sugimoto (2018), Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics 3:17, DOI 10.3389/frma.2018.00017, compares global mobility and collaboration networks and finds that country positions diverge most for lower-income countries. El Ouahi, Robinson-García & Costas (2021), QSS 2(3), DOI 10.1162/qss_a_00149, does the same for MENA, finding different hubs in the two layers. Earlier, Halevi & Moed (2012, arXiv 1212.5194) and Moed, Aisati & Plume (2013, Scientometrics 94(3), DOI 10.1007/s11192-012-0783-9) reported that scientific migration patterns differ from co-authorship patterns, with language and proximity mattering more for migration. All of these define 'migration' as bibliometric scholarly mobility. None uses general-population migrant stocks (UN DESA), formal distributional divergence (JSD, top-k overlap, rank correlation) per origin, or degree- and strength-preserving null models, and none focuses on Sub-Saharan origins beyond Somalia's inclusion in the travel-ban set.

(b) Comparing general migration with scholarly mobility as predictors of collaboration. No paper was found that enters UN DESA total bilateral stocks and bibliometric scholarly-migration flows side by side in a co-authorship gravity model. The closest are:
- Noumedem Temgoua (2018), GREThA WP 2018-16, 'Highly skilled migration and the internationalization of knowledge'. It runs a gravity model (PPML per the working-paper text) of OECD country-pair co-authorship and co-inventorship on Chinese and Indian highly skilled diaspora stocks while controlling for other migration variables, so skilled diaspora is separated from general migration, but on destination-destination dyads.
- Miguélez (2018), World Bank Economic Review 32(1), DOI 10.1093/wber/lhw013. The patent analogue, with inventor-diaspora stocks in gravity models of co-patenting.
- Kato & Ando (2017), Scientometrics 110(2), DOI 10.1007/s11192-016-2183-z. Count-data country-pair models showing that researcher mobility predicts collaboration, with one-way causation from mobility to collaboration.
- Doria Arrieta, Pammolli & Petersen (2017), Science Advances 3(4): e1602232. Official high-skilled mobility imbalance reduced EU cross-border collaboration.
- Appelt et al. (2015), OECD STI WP 2015/2. The reverse direction: co-authorship and reverse student flows predict bilateral scientist mobility, which implies scholarly mobility is endogenous to collaboration.
Individual-level causal work on African and developing-country scientists (Fry 2023, Organization Science, DOI 10.1287/orsc.2022.1580; Fry & Furman 2025, DOI 10.1287/orsc.2023.1683; Ito et al. 2025, Journal of Development Economics, DOI 10.1016/j.jdeveco.2025.103577) indicates that the collaboration-generating channel is science-specific mobility (trained researchers, returnees, mobile PhDs) rather than diaspora size per se. That is consistent with the project's hypothesis but has not been tested at the country-pair level against general migrant stocks.

Caveats: DOIs were verified only through WebSearch snippets and summaries, because api.crossref.org and cahiersdugretha.u-bordeaux.fr were blocked for WebFetch, and all findings are abstract-level.

papers.title: Gone but not forgotten: knowledge flows, labor mobility, and enduring social relationships
papers.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Iain Cockburn, John McHale
papers.research_question: After an inventor moves away, do the social relationships they built while co-located keep sending knowledge flows (patent citations) back to their former location?

papers.title: Foreign-origin inventors in the USA: testing for diaspora and brain gain effects

The effect weakens as interactions become more formal, and is stronger for inventor-to-inventor co-inventorship than for applicant-to-inventor links. The Chinese and Indian diasporas do not drive the results.

Our design swaps in UN DESA total migrant stocks and Akbaritabar scholarly mobility to test whether the general diaspora or the skilled or scholarly subset carries the effect.

papers.title: Inventor migration and knowledge flows: A two-way communication channel?
papers.authors: Ernest Miguelez, Claudia Noumedem Temgoua
papers.research_question: Does inventor migration raise knowledge flows in both directions, back to home countries and into host countries?
papers.data: Country-pair data for 1990-2010 on inventor migration and international patent citations (abstract-level).
papers.methods: Country-pair gravity model of cross-country patent citations, with instrumental variables and country-pair fixed effects.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. Inventor migration robustly increases knowledge flows to home countries under IV and pair fixed effects. The effect on flows into host countries does not hold up. The effects matter mainly when sending countries are developing countries and for knowledge diffusion within multinationals.
papers.relevance_to_project: Shows that the knowledge payoff of migration is directional and concentrated in developing origins, which is relevant to SSA. Supports keeping direction (origin to destination) in the mobility and migrant-stock layers even though co-authorship is undirected, and testing for asymmetry in residuals.

papers.title: Migration, Knowledge Diffusion and the Comparative Advantage of Nations
papers.authors: Dany Bahar, Hillel Rapoport
papers.research_question: Does international migration spread tacit productive knowledge, shown by countries starting to export new products?
papers.data: Bilateral migration stocks and product-level export data across countries (abstract-level). Earlier versions: IZA DP 9788 and CESifo WP 5769.
papers.methods: Relates migrant stocks from a product's exporters to the probability that the host country starts exporting that product within ten years. Migration is instrumented in a gravity framework.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. A 10% increase in immigrants from countries that export a product is associated with roughly a 2% higher probability that the host country starts exporting it within a decade. Effects are stronger for highly skilled migrants, qualitatively similar for emigrants, and robust to gravity-based instrumentation.
papers.relevance_to_project: Evidence that generic bilateral migrant stocks carry knowledge in the productive or trade domain. That makes it a direct contrast for testing whether the same stocks carry scientific knowledge. The gravity-predicted migration instrument could be reused to address endogeneity in co-authorship PPML.

papers.title: Globalization, Brain Drain, and Development

papers.research_question: What do four decades of research say about the size, causes and development consequences of high-skill emigration?

papers.title: Network Approach versus Brain Drain: Lessons from the Diaspora
papers.authors: Jean-Baptiste Meyer

papers.title: The International-Migration Network
papers.authors: Giorgio Fagiolo, Marina Mastrorillo
papers.venue: arXiv:1212.3852 / LEM Working Paper 2012/23. The published version appears to be Physical Review E 88:012812 (2013), but the journal title wording was not confirmed.
papers.research_question: What is the binary and weighted topology of the international migration network, how did it change between 1960 and 2000, and can a gravity model account for it?
papers.data: Bilateral migrant stocks from origin to destination countries, 1960-2000, treated as a weighted directed graph (abstract-level).
papers.methods: Network statistics on the weighted directed migrant-stock network, compared against a parsimonious gravity model of migration.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. The network is modular, with a small-world pattern, disassortative mixing, high clustering and power-law distributed weighted statistics. A parsimonious gravity model accounts for most of the observed topology, and socio-economic, geographical and political factors matter more than local network properties.
papers.relevance_to_project: Baseline topology of a migrant-stock layer of the same type as UN DESA. Shows that gravity models reproduce much of the migration topology, which supports using gravity-based expectations alongside degree- or strength-preserving nulls in the multilayer comparison.
papers.verification_source: The arXiv 1212.3852 and LEM WP 2012/23 records were seen via WebSearch. A link.aps.org result for 10.1103/PhysRevE.88.012812 (2013) appeared for this author pair, but its title match was not confirmed, so the DOI field is left null. The candidate DOI should be checked before citing.

established: Inventor and patent studies show that social ties formed through co-location outlast mobility. Agrawal, Cockburn and McHale (2006) find knowledge flows to a mobile inventor's former location are about 50% larger than the counterfactual.

Skilled diasporas are associated with knowledge flows and co-invention with their origin countries. Kerr (2008) uses ethnic patent citations. Miguelez (2018) finds diasporas are associated with co-patenting with developing and emerging economies, with the effect weakening as interactions become more formal. Miguelez and Noumedem Temgoua (2020) find migration raises knowledge flows back to home countries, mainly for developing origins.

A diaspora effect inside the destination does not automatically become a gain for the origin country. Breschi, Lissoni and Miguelez (2017) find no brain gain for India. Agrawal et al. (2011) find a net harm to domestic knowledge access, although diaspora access matters for top inventions. Co-invention networks and multinationals outweigh diaspora channels.

Generic bilateral migrant stocks predict economic ties: new exports and comparative advantage (Bahar and Rapoport 2018) and trade, with causal evidence from refugee dispersal (Parsons and Vezina 2018). Effects are stronger for skilled migrants.

High-skill emigration need not deplete origin human capital and can create network externalities (Docquier and Rapoport 2012). The scientific diaspora and brain circulation literatures (Meyer and Brown 1999; Meyer 2001; Saxenian 2005) frame diaspora knowledge networks as organized, selective subsets of migrants rather than the whole migrant stock.

Complex-network studies find that migration layers are strongly correlated with trade and FDI layers, but mostly because of country size and distance. Migration-network centrality adds explanatory power in gravity models (Fagiolo and Mastrorillo 2014; Sgrignoli et al. 2015; Garas et al. 2016). Gravity models reproduce much of the migration network's own topology (Fagiolo and Mastrorillo, arXiv 1212.3852).
unresolved: No study found here compares general migrant stocks, scholarly mobility and co-authorship as separate country-pair layers for the same origins. The diaspora-knowledge literature mostly uses skill-specific or name-identified inventor diasporas, not total UN DESA stocks.

Evidence is concentrated on Chinese, Indian and European diasporas and OECD destinations. Sub-Saharan African origins, and refugee-driven diasporas such as Somalia, Ethiopia and Rwanda, are almost absent from patent and diaspora-knowledge studies.
It is unclear whether results for patents and co-patenting carry over to scientific co-authorship. Patenting is rare for SSA, so co-authorship may be the only usable knowledge layer.

The cross-layer correlations in migration-trade and migration-FDI networks are largely explained by gravity. It is open whether any migration-knowledge alignment survives degree- or strength-preserving nulls and gravity residualization.

Directionality: knowledge-flow effects appear asymmetric, toward home countries (Miguelez and Noumedem Temgoua 2020). How to reconcile directed migration and mobility layers with undirected co-authorship counts remains a design question.

Name-based ethnicity methods (Kerr 2008; Breschi et al. 2017) are validated mainly for Asian and European names. Their reliability for African names, and therefore for identifying SSA scientific diasporas, is unclear.

Verification caveats: api.crossref.org and academic.oup.com were unreachable, so this session could not read pages directly and all checks went through WebSearch result snippets. The Agrawal et al. (2011) DOI rests on a third-party aggregator listing. The Saxenian (2005) DOI rests on a doi.org search hit. The Physical Review E version of Fagiolo and Mastrorillo's migration-network paper (candidate DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.88.012812) still needs a title check. To check DOIs directly against Crossref, api.crossref.org has to be allowed in the session's network settings.
Meyer and Brown (1999) was seen only at record and introduction level. Its inventory of networks and its specific findings were not read.
sweep.closest_prior_work_to_our_contribution: Two strands come closest, and neither matches the project's design. On the econometric side, Miguelez (2018, WBER) runs gravity models of international co-patenting on inventor-diaspora stocks for developing and emerging origins. That is a direct analogue of a PPML co-authorship gravity model with migrant stocks. Breschi, Lissoni and Miguelez (2017, JEG) and Miguelez and Noumedem Temgoua (2020, Research Policy) show that diaspora presence does not automatically produce origin-destination knowledge ties and that the effects are directional, which is close to the 'migration network is not the knowledge network' thesis. On the network side, Fagiolo and Mastrorillo (2014, PLoS ONE), Sgrignoli et al. (2015, Physica A, hypergeometric filter of over-represented links) and Garas et al. (2016, ACS) compare a migration layer with an economic layer (trade or FDI) and find overlap that gravity largely explains. None of these compares total UN DESA migrant stocks, bibliometric scholarly mobility and co-authorship as three layers, uses per-origin distributional alignment measures (rank correlation, top-k overlap, Jensen-Shannon divergence) against degree- or strength-preserving nulls, or focuses on Sub-Saharan African origins. Those are the project's distinct contributions.

papers.title: Bilateral flows and rates of international migration of scholars for 210 countries for the period 1998-2020
papers.authors: Aliakbar Akbaritabar, Tom Theile, Emilio Zagheni
papers.research_question: How can publication metadata be used to estimate yearly international migration rates and bilateral flows of publishing scholars for all countries, and how consistent are the estimates across Scopus and OpenAlex?
papers.data: Bibliometric metadata from Scopus and OpenAlex. One summary says more than 36 million articles and reviews were used, but that figure may refer to the Scopus base used in the authors' related work. Country-level aggregated yearly rates and bilateral origin-to-destination flows for 210 countries and areas, 1998-2020. Earlier version: MPIDR Working Paper WP-2023-018, 'Global flows and rates of international migration of scholars'.
papers.methods: Scholars are tracked over time through the countries of their publication affiliations. A slide deck from the group says a scholar's yearly country of residence is the modal country of their affiliations that year; I could not confirm this wording in the paper itself. Changes in that country count as migration events. The authors set out pre-processing steps and best practices for identifying migration, then aggregate to yearly rates and bilateral flows, and cross-validate scholar counts between Scopus and OpenAlex.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Scholar counts in Scopus and OpenAlex are highly correlated for most countries. OpenAlex covers non-Western countries more extensively, but agreement with Scopus is highest in Western countries. A secondary source (OpenAlex blog) adds two points: migration events are less correlated between the two sources than scholar counts, although trends for the top country pairs are consistent, and flow magnitudes are much larger in OpenAlex than in Scopus. A later version (SMD 2.0, WP-2026-029) extends coverage to 1998-2024 with gender, field and subnational breakdowns.
papers.relevance_to_project: This is layer (2) of the project, the scholarly mobility flows. Limitations to plan around: (a) it covers only scholars who publish and are indexed, and inferred moves depend on affiliation strings and author disambiguation; (b) it is a flow measure, while UN DESA gives stocks; (c) the Scopus and OpenAlex versions disagree more for non-Western, including Sub-Saharan African, countries, and absolute flow levels are much higher in OpenAlex, so robustness checks should use both sources; (d) small origins such as Somalia and Rwanda will have sparse rows and many zeros, which suits PPML but makes rank and divergence metrics noisy. A further caution: co-authorship and mobility are both built from the same affiliation metadata (OpenAlex), so some alignment between layers (2) and (3) could be mechanical, especially where affiliation changes and multiple affiliations are confused.

papers.research_question: How common is international researcher mobility, and how is mobility associated with citation impact across countries and regions?

papers.findings: From secondary and press summaries; I did not see the full text. About 96% of authors were non-mobile and about 4% mobile. The authors argue that restricting circulation harms science. Commentators note the result is correlational, since selection into mobility is not ruled out.

It shows that bibliometric mobility covers a small, selective share of researchers, which helps explain why the scholarly mobility layer can diverge from general migrant stocks. It does not model co-authorship partner distributions.

papers.title: The many faces of mobility: Using bibliometric data to measure the movement of scientists
papers.authors: Nicolas Robinson-Garcia, Cassidy R. Sugimoto, Dakota Murray, Alfredo Yegros-Yegros, Vincent Lariviere, Rodrigo Costas
papers.research_question: How can publication affiliation data be used to build a typology and indicators of scientific mobility?
papers.data: About 16 million authors in Web of Science, 2008-2015 (arXiv preprint 1803.03449).
papers.methods: A typology of mobility based on affiliation sequences. 'Migrants' break ties with their origin country. 'Travelers' add foreign affiliations while keeping origin ties, and are split into directional and non-directional. Country-level incoming and outgoing classifications are also built.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. About 3.7% of authors were mobile. Travelers make up most mobile scholars (72.7% per one summary), but migrants have higher scientific impact; impact ranks migrants first, then directional travelers, non-directional travelers and non-mobile researchers.
papers.relevance_to_project: Key for interpreting the Akbaritabar flows. Multiple and concurrent affiliations ('travelers') sit on the boundary between mobility and collaboration. A traveler with a home affiliation and a foreign affiliation produces co-authorship-like cross-country links, so the scholarly mobility layer and the co-authorship layer are not independent. The paper's directional typology supports treating origin-to-destination direction explicitly rather than symmetrising.

papers.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics 3, article 17
papers.research_question: How do international mobility networks and international collaboration networks relate across countries with different scientific and technological capacity?

In the more prolific countries, flows of mobile researchers are significantly related to publishing with foreign partners, but mobility is always lower than collaboration. It compares mobility and collaboration networks at country level and finds weaker correspondence for lower-capacity countries, which is the regime of most Sub-Saharan origins. The project extends it by adding UN DESA general migrant stocks as a third layer, by using per-origin distributional alignment (rank correlation, top-k overlap, JSD) with null models, and by PPML gravity models.

papers.research_question: What economic, geographic, scientific and policy factors explain bilateral flows of research scientists between countries?
papers.data: A new mobility measure from changes in affiliations reported by publishing scientists in a major global index of scholarly publications (Scopus), 1996-2011, bilateral country pairs.
papers.methods: Gravity-model estimation of bilateral scientist mobility flows, with distance terms (geographic, socioeconomic, scientific), economic and R&D conditions, visa restrictions, collaboration intensity and reverse-direction student flows.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. Geographic, socioeconomic and scientific distance are negatively associated with scientist mobility between two countries. Scientific collaboration appears to be a major factor linked to mobility. Mobility increases with converging economic conditions and R&D resources, and is lower with visa restrictions. Scientist mobility is strongly associated with tertiary student flows in the opposite direction, which the authors read as multi-directional brain circulation.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest gravity-model precedent. It shows collaboration and mobility are linked dyadically, which raises endogeneity concerns for the project's PPML specification (co-authorship regressed on mobility). It also shows that direction matters: the reverse student-flow result suggests including both directions of mobility and migrant stocks in dyadic models.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch result list showed www.doi.org/10.1787/5JS1TMRR2233-EN (OECD STI Working Papers) and the OECD iLibrary URL '..._5js1tmrr2233-en' with this exact title; EconPapers record RePEc:oec:stiaaa:2015/2-en.

papers.title: The globalisation of scientific mobility, 1970-2014
papers.authors: Mathias Czaika, Sultan Orazbayev
papers.venue: Applied Geography 96, 1-10 (the task brief's attribution to Research Policy appears to be wrong)
papers.research_question: How has global scientific mobility changed over four decades, in geographic range, centre of gravity and distance, and what are its bilateral determinants, including visa restrictions?
papers.data: Bibliometric data on scientists' affiliation changes, 1970-2014; citing work describes it as Scopus. Also IMI Working Paper 146 (2018).
papers.methods: Descriptive network and geography analysis of bilateral scientific mobility; citing work reports gravity-type regressions including visa restrictions.
papers.findings: Abstract-level (Growth Lab and IMI pages). The range of origin and destination countries has widened. The centre of gravity of scientific production and migration destinations has shifted eastward. Average migration distances have grown as peripheral regions join the global science system. Visa restrictions are a statistically significant barrier to scientists' mobility. A citing source says scientists were found to be about three times as internationally mobile as non-scientists; this is not confirmed from the abstract.
papers.relevance_to_project: Supports including visa and policy-barrier covariates and long-run trends. The finding that scientists are far more mobile than the general population, if confirmed, implies scholarly mobility flows and UN DESA migrant stocks should differ in scale and probably in geography.
papers.verification_source: Title, authors and venue (Applied Geography 96, July 2018, pp. 1-10) confirmed via the Harvard Growth Lab listing, the ScienceDirect PII S0143622817305428 URL in search results, and Scinapse. One search summary reported DOI 10.1016/j.apgeog.2018.04.017, but my query already contained that string and a follow-up search did not confirm it, so doi is left null. Check before citing.

papers.title: Multiscale impact of researcher mobility
papers.authors: Alexander M. Petersen
papers.venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface 15(146), 20180580
papers.research_question: What are the effects of cross-border researcher mobility on citation impact, topic diversity, collaboration and international integration?
papers.data: American Physical Society journals 1980-2009; 26,170 disambiguated prominent researcher profiles (dataset on Dryad).
papers.methods: Matching mobile researchers to similar non-mobile researchers on pre-move profile attributes, followed by a 10-year window around each move. Outcomes cover individual impact, co-author diversity, collaboration network churn and international integration, across three time periods.
papers.findings: Abstract and summary level. Mobile researchers gain up to a 17% citation advantage, attributed to a simultaneous increase in co-author diversity. Researchers completely curtail prior collaborations with their source country in 11% of cross-border moves. Effects appear across scales, from careers to collaboration network churn to international integration, and virtual channels do not appear to replace physical mobility.
papers.relevance_to_project: One of the few studies that directly links a move to later co-authorship. Most movers keep ties to the origin country (only 11% fully curtail them), so the mobility layer should predict origin-destination co-authorship in both directions, while collaboration networks also churn after moves. It covers physics only, mostly in high-income systems.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results included PMC6170771 with title 'Multiscale impact of researcher mobility'; the search summary gave J R Soc Interface 15(146):20180580, DOI 10.1098/rsif.2018.0580, sole author A. M. Petersen. My query did not contain the DOI.

papers.title: Talent goes to global cities: The world network of scientists' mobility
papers.authors: Luca Verginer, Massimo Riccaboni
papers.research_question: How is the world network of scientists' mobility structured at city level, and do global cities attract and retain the most productive scientists?
papers.data: Disambiguated author publication histories at city level. The full-text PDF describes 3.7 million authors and 7,159 cities; another summary says about 2 million researchers and more than 2,000 cities over a decade. The source database is not confirmed from what I saw.
papers.methods: Construction of a city-level mobility network and analysis of the centrality of global cities, plus the productivity of scientists they attract and retain.
papers.findings: Abstract and full-text fragments. Global cities attract and retain the most productive scientists, benefiting from their central position in the international mobility network by attracting and retaining prolific scientists early in their careers.
papers.relevance_to_project: Shows that scholarly mobility concentrates on a few hubs, which matters for the multilayer topology comparison and for strength-preserving nulls, since hub concentration may differ from the more diffuse geography of general migrant stocks. City-level work also warns that country aggregation hides within-country concentration.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results showed the ETH research-collection record and the IDEAS record (eee/respol v50y2021i1 s004873332030202x) with this title; the search summary gave DOI 10.1016/j.respol.2020.104127 and Research Policy 50(1) 104127. The PDF filename (S004873332030202X) matches the PII.

papers.title: Open countries have strong science
papers.authors: Caroline S. Wagner, Koen Jonkers
papers.research_question: Is a country's openness to international engagement, through collaboration and researcher mobility, associated with the impact of its science?
papers.data: Country-level indicators for a set of leading scientific countries: share of internationally co-authored papers and researcher mobility (inflows and outflows), plus citation impact.
papers.methods: Construction of an openness index combining international collaboration and mobility, and correlation of openness with citation impact. A 2018 follow-up ('Openness and Impact of Leading Scientific Countries', arXiv 1810.07812) extends it.
papers.findings: From secondary sources and the follow-up. There is a clear correlation between a nation's scientific influence and its links with foreign researchers: more open countries produce higher-impact science. The follow-up warns that the correlation does not imply all countries have equal potential to open up, and that results do not extend to unanalysed countries.
papers.relevance_to_project: Treats collaboration and mobility as two parts of one openness construct, a framing the project questions. It covers only leading countries, not Sub-Saharan Africa, so its pooling of mobility and collaboration may not hold for peripheral origins.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch result list showed the IDEAS record URL nat/nature v550y2017i7674 d10.1038_550032a; the search summary gave the title 'Open countries have strong science', Nature 550(7674):32-33.

papers.title: Return migration of German-affiliated researchers: analyzing departure and return by gender, cohort, and discipline using Scopus bibliometric data 1996-2020
papers.authors: Xinyi Zhao, Samin Aref, Emilio Zagheni, Guy Stecklov
papers.research_question: Who among researchers who leave Germany returns, and how does return vary by gender, cohort, discipline, destination and continued collaboration with German-affiliated researchers?
papers.data: Scopus: about 8 million publications by about 1.1 million researchers who published at least once with a German affiliation, 1996-2020 (arXiv 2110.08340).
papers.methods: Bibliometric identification of departure and return events from affiliation histories, with descriptive cohort analysis and models of return propensity including collaboration ties to Germany while abroad.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. Return migration declines slightly in more recent cohorts, which for most disciplines coincides with fewer German collaboration ties. Women who leave are less likely than men to return. Keeping collaborations with German-affiliated researchers while abroad has a moderate positive association with return. Per a Population Europe digest, those who moved to high R&D-spending countries were less likely to return.
papers.relevance_to_project: Evidence that collaboration ties with the origin persist after emigration and predict return, so knowledge links run in both directions along migration corridors. It supports modelling both directions of mobility and treating origin-destination co-authorship as partly a diaspora tie. It is a single-origin case in a high-income country.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results (MPIDR journal-article page, arXiv 2110.08340, Population Europe) showed this title; the search summary gave Scientometrics 127(12):7707-7729 and DOI 10.1007/s11192-022-04351-4. My query did not contain the DOI.

papers.title: The demography of the peripatetic researcher: Evidence on highly mobile scholars from the Web of Science
papers.authors: Samin Aref, Emilio Zagheni, Jevin West
papers.venue: Social Informatics (SocInfo 2019), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 11864, Springer, pp. 50-65
papers.research_question: Who are the highly mobile ('peripatetic') researchers who publish from three or more countries, and what global structure do their moves form?
papers.data: Main affiliation addresses on more than 62 million Web of Science publications, 1956-2016 (arXiv 1907.13414).
papers.methods: Tracking researchers' affiliation countries over time; defining super-movers as those with publications from at least three distinct countries; demographic and network description.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. More than 90% of researchers show no international mobility. Peripatetic researchers form a global system with the USA and China as two large hubs and England and Germany as two smaller hubs. The paper frames the policy debate as shifting from brain drain to brain circulation.
papers.relevance_to_project: Methodological precursor to the MPIDR scholarly migration database. It shows that bibliometric mobility is rare and hub-concentrated, which supports degree- and strength-preserving nulls in the topology comparison.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch result list showed link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-34971-4_4 titled 'The Demography of the Peripatetic Researcher: Evidence on Highly Mobile Scholars from the Web of Science'; Altmetric and Unpaywall entries gave the same DOI. Note the DOI suffix is _4, not _3.

papers.title: Migrant scientists and international networks
papers.authors: Giuseppe Scellato, Chiara Franzoni, Paula Stephan
papers.research_question: Do migrant scientists have more international research networks than non-migrants and returnees, and do they keep collaborating with their country of origin?
papers.data: GlobSci survey (2011) of corresponding authors in 16 countries in four fields, comparing foreign-born scientists, non-migrants and returnees. NBER WP 18613 version: 'Mobile Scientists and International Networks'.
papers.methods: Survey-based comparison and regression of international collaboration incidence by migrant status, training path and origin-country science base.
papers.findings: Abstract-level. Migrants have a higher incidence of international collaboration, driven mainly by those who did their PhD abroad and then moved for a postdoc or job. A sizeable share of foreign-born scientists collaborate with researchers in their country of origin; the NBER version reports about 40% keep research links with origin colleagues. Migrants from countries with stronger science bases have better networks.
papers.relevance_to_project: Direct micro-evidence linking migration to later co-authorship with the origin country. The finding that origin science capacity conditions network strength predicts that, for weak-capacity origins such as Somalia or Rwanda, large migrant stocks may translate weakly into origin-destination co-authorship. This supports interacting migrant stock with origin research capacity in PPML.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results showed the EconPapers record eee:respol v44 i1 p108-120 and POLITO/POLIMI repository entries with this title; the search summary gave DOI 10.1016/j.respol.2014.07.014. My query did not contain the DOI.

papers.title: Foreign-born scientists: mobility patterns for 16 countries
papers.authors: Chiara Franzoni, Giuseppe Scellato, Paula Stephan
papers.research_question: What shares of scientists are foreign-born across 16 core research countries, and what are their mobility patterns and reasons for moving?
papers.data: GlobSci survey: corresponding authors of 2009 articles in four fields (including biology, chemistry, earth and environmental sciences, and materials) working in 16 countries; 17,182 respondents in 2011. NBER WP 18067.
papers.methods: Cross-national survey of migration history, country of origin and reasons for mobility.
papers.findings: Abstract and summary level. Switzerland had the highest share of immigrant scientists; India had the lowest, closely followed by Italy and Japan. There was wide cross-country variation in foreign-born shares and in emigration patterns.
papers.relevance_to_project: The main survey benchmark (GlobSci) against which bibliometric mobility estimates can be compared. It covers 16 mostly high-income countries and no Sub-Saharan origins as host countries, so it shows a coverage gap the bibliometric data partly fill.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch result list contained dx.doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2449, and the search summary matched it to this title in Nature Biotechnology 30(12):1250-1253 (published 7 Dec 2012). A Scilit entry and NBER w18067 share the title. Not cross-checked on Crossref (blocked).

established: Bibliometric mobility is rare and selective. Only about 4% of WoS authors (Sugimoto et al. 2017), about 3.7% (Robinson-Garcia et al. 2019), and fewer than 10% (Aref et al. 2019) show international mobility, concentrated in a few hubs (USA, China, England, Germany; global cities per Verginer & Riccaboni 2021). The scholarly mobility layer covers a very different population from UN DESA migrant stocks.

Mobility and collaboration are related but not interchangeable. In prolific countries mobile-researcher flows correlate with foreign co-publication, but mobility is always lower than collaboration, and country rankings diverge especially for lower-income countries (Chinchilla-Rodriguez et al. 2018, Frontiers). Advanced countries show closer alignment of mobility and collaboration networks than lagging countries (Pei et al. 2024).

Migration and co-authorship have different determinants. Language similarity matters more for migration than for co-authorship (Moed, Aisati & Plume 2013). Affinity and asymmetry indexes reveal discrepancies between collaboration and mobility at the dyad level, including for Somalia and other travel-ban countries (Chinchilla-Rodriguez et al. 2018, Scientometrics).

Gravity logic applies to scholarly mobility. Geographic, socioeconomic and scientific distance reduce bilateral scientist flows, visa restrictions are a barrier, and collaboration intensity is a major correlate (Appelt et al. 2015; Czaika & Orazbayev 2018).

Direction matters. Scientist mobility is associated with student flows in the opposite direction (Appelt et al. 2015). Asymmetry indexes capture directional imbalance (Chinchilla-Rodriguez et al. 2018). Directional and non-directional travelers differ in impact (Robinson-Garcia et al. 2019).

Moves are followed by persistent origin ties and by collaboration churn. Only about 11% of cross-border movers completely curtail collaboration with the source country (Petersen 2018). About 40% of foreign-born scientists keep research links with the origin, more so when the origin has a stronger science base (Scellato, Franzoni & Stephan 2015). Keeping origin collaborations is positively associated with return (Zhao et al. 2022).

Mobile scientists have higher citation impact (about 40% higher in WoS, Sugimoto et al. 2017; up to 17% in APS physics with matching, Petersen 2018), but selection is not ruled out. Openness, combining collaboration and mobility, correlates with national impact among leading countries (Wagner & Jonkers 2017).

The MPIDR scholarly migration flows (Akbaritabar, Theile & Zagheni 2024) show strong Scopus-OpenAlex agreement in scholar counts for most countries, weakest for non-Western countries. OpenAlex has broader non-Western coverage and much larger flow magnitudes, and migration events agree less across sources than counts do (the last point from a secondary source).
unresolved: I found no study that puts general-population bilateral migrant stocks (UN DESA) alongside bibliometric scholarly mobility and co-authorship in one origin-specific comparison or gravity model, especially for Sub-Saharan origins. Diaspora and ethnic-tie co-authorship literature (e.g. Kerr; Freeman & Huang; Agrawal, Kapur & McHale) was outside this topic's scope and should be checked by another reviewer before claiming novelty.

Causal direction between mobility and collaboration is contested. Kato & Ando (2017, Scientometrics 110(2), DOI 10.1007/s11192-016-2183-z, seen via search listing) report mobility leading to collaboration. Liu & Hu (2021, J Informetrics 15(1) 101113) find collaborators predict later moves among Chinese scientists. A MENA Scopus study reportedly finds bidirectional effects (not identified or verified). The project's PPML with mobility as a regressor therefore faces simultaneity.

The Akbaritabar et al. 2024 methods details (yearly modal-country residence rule, minimum publication thresholds, handling of concurrent multiple affiliations, author disambiguation error rates, treatment of first-publication 'entries') could not be read because nature.com, PMC and Crossref were network-blocked. These details determine how much of the mobility layer is mechanically co-produced with OpenAlex co-authorship and should be read from the paper.

It is untested whether OpenAlex affiliation noise for African institutions inflates or deflates SSA scholarly flows and co-authorship, given that Scopus-OpenAlex agreement is weakest outside the West.

Jonkers & Cruz-Castro (2013, Research Policy 42(8):1366-1377), 'Research upon return', is relevant to return mobility and later collaboration (Argentina): foreign experience is linked to higher-impact publishing, much of it without international co-authorship. Sources conflicted on its DOI (10.1016/j.respol.2013.05.005 vs 10.1016/j.respol.2013.03.012), so it was not included as verified.
Czaika & Orazbayev (2018) is in Applied Geography 96:1-10, not Research Policy as the brief states. Its DOI (candidate 10.1016/j.apgeog.2018.04.017) was not independently confirmed.

Newer work could not be read beyond secondary sources. Yenilmez (2026, Applied Network Science 11, art. 65, DOI 10.1007/s41109-026-00840-0, title-DOI match seen in a search listing) reportedly finds the 1974-2023 Scopus academic migration network highly reciprocal ('circulatory'). Zegarra (2026, Scientometrics, DOI 10.1007/s11192-026-05752-5 seen in a search listing) compares mobility and co-authorship views for Peru, Colombia and Venezuela. Both are relevant to reciprocity nulls and peripheral-country comparisons but are unverified at abstract level.

Related MPIDR papers not included in the 16: Sanliturk et al. (2023, PNAS 120(4) e2217937120, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2217937120) find a U-shaped relation between scholars' emigration rates and GDP per capita, turning near $25,000 PPP. This is a useful covariate idea for origin heterogeneity.
sweep.closest_prior_work_to_our_contribution: The closest work is Chinchilla-Rodriguez, Miao, Murray, Robinson-Garcia, Costas & Sugimoto (2018), 'A Global Comparison of Scientific Mobility and Collaboration According to National Scientific Capacities' (Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics 3:17, DOI 10.3389/frma.2018.00017). Using WoS 2008-2015 affiliation data, it compares country-level mobility and collaboration networks across capacity tiers. Mobility tracks collaboration in prolific countries but is always lower, and rankings diverge most for lower-income, lagging countries. Two other papers are close: Pei, Li, Yang & Zhou (2024, Scientometrics 129(7), DOI 10.1007/s11192-024-05081-5) find closer mobility-collaboration network alignment for advanced than lagging countries, and Chinchilla-Rodriguez, Bu et al. (2018, Scientometrics 116(1), DOI 10.1007/s11192-018-2738-2) use size-normalised affinity and asymmetry indexes to show dyad-level discrepancies between collaboration and mobility for the travel-ban countries, including Somalia. Moed, Aisati & Plume (2013) give early evidence that migration and co-authorship differ in their determinants (language), and Appelt et al. (2015) give the gravity-model template. None of these, as far as I could confirm, adds general-population UN DESA migrant stocks as a third layer, uses per-origin distributional alignment (rank correlation, top-k overlap, Jensen-Shannon divergence) with null models, or runs PPML co-authorship gravity with both migrant stocks and the Akbaritabar et al. (2024) scholarly flows for Sub-Saharan origins. That combination is the project's apparent contribution. Verification caveat: only WebSearch worked; api.crossref.org and nature.com were network-blocked for WebFetch, so DOI checks rely on search-result listings and summaries. Allowing those hosts would enable direct Crossref confirmation.
