papers.title: Network structure, self-organization, and the growth of international collaboration in science
papers.authors: Caroline S. Wagner; Loet Leydesdorff
papers.research_question: Why has international co-authorship grown so fast, and is the growth better explained by network self-organization (preferential attachment) than by national policy or funding?
papers.data: International co-authorship links between countries, built from bibliometric (ISI/Web of Science) records. Abstract-level only; the exact years were not checked.
papers.methods: Network analysis of the country co-authorship network, including degree distributions and tests of preferential attachment / self-organization.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. The authors describe international collaboration as a self-organizing network whose growth follows network dynamics (preferential attachment to well-connected countries) more than national or institutional incentives.
papers.relevance_to_project: This is the standard framing of the country-level co-authorship layer as a self-organizing network. It explains why the knowledge layer may follow its own core-periphery logic rather than the migration layer, which motivates the degree/strength-preserving null models and the multilayer topology comparison.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: Scilit record (scilit.net) giving https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2005.08.002 with Research Policy 34(10):1608-1618, and the EconPapers RePEc handle for the same volume, issue and pages.

papers.title: The continuing growth of global cooperation networks in research: A conundrum for national governments
papers.authors: Caroline S. Wagner; Han Woo Park; Loet Leydesdorff
papers.research_question: How has the global network of international co-authorship evolved, and what does its growth mean for national science policy?
papers.data: Internationally co-authored publications between countries over about two decades (bibliometric database). Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Network analysis of country co-authorship networks over time.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. The share of internationally co-authored papers has more than doubled in 20 years and accounts for the output growth of advanced countries. The network acts as a new organization alongside national systems. Emerging countries, especially China, are participating more. International collaboration does not appear to threaten national science and may improve its quality.
papers.relevance_to_project: Background on the growth and densification of the co-authorship layer. Its claim that the network is a supranational structure supports testing whether co-authorship partners diverge from migration corridors.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: PubMed Central record PMC4510583 and DOAJ/library catalogue records reporting DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0131816, published 21 July 2015.

papers.title: National characteristics in international scientific co-authorship relations
papers.authors: Wolfgang Glänzel
papers.research_question: What national characteristics shape international co-authorship? Are bilateral co-publication links symmetric, and how does international collaboration relate to national research profiles and citation impact?
papers.data: International co-authored publications by country (ISI databases, 1990s). Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Bibliometric indicators of bilateral co-authorship strength, with symmetry/asymmetry tests of country-pair links and field-level citation analysis.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Not all bilateral links are symmetric. Internationally co-authored papers are cited more on average than domestic ones, but the citation gain from international collaboration varies a lot between countries and, within countries, between fields.
papers.relevance_to_project: The asymmetry of country-pair links matters directly when comparing directed migration stocks and directed scholarly mobility flows with undirected co-authorship. It supports normalizing per origin (each origin's partner distribution) rather than using raw symmetric counts.

papers.title: Research collaboration at a distance: Changing spatial patterns of scientific collaboration within Europe
papers.authors: Jarno Hoekman; Koen Frenken; Robert J. W. Tijssen
papers.research_question: How do physical distance and territorial borders (regional, national, linguistic) affect research collaboration between European regions, and has their effect changed over time?
papers.data: All co-publications between 313 regions in 33 European countries, 2000-2007 (Web of Science).
papers.methods: Gravity equation of co-publication counts between regions, with distance and border/language dummies, estimated over time.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. European integration is weakening the effect of territorial borders, but sensitivity to physical distance has not fallen, so the preference for nearby partners persists. Collaboration propensity varies a lot between regions and countries, which the authors relate to size, quality and accessibility.
papers.relevance_to_project: A key methodological precedent for count-based gravity models of co-publication with distance, language and border terms. It provides baseline covariates and expected signs for the PPML co-authorship model before migrant stocks and scholarly mobility are added.

papers.title: Proximity dimensions and scientific collaboration among academic institutions in Europe: The closer, the better?
papers.authors: Ana Fernández; Esther Ferrándiz; María Dolores León
papers.research_question: Which proximity dimensions (geographical, cognitive, institutional, organizational, social, economic) explain co-authorship between European universities?

papers.title: Globalization of science and international scientific collaboration: A network perspective
papers.authors: Qinchang Gui; Chengliang Liu; Debin Du
papers.research_question: How did the global international scientific collaboration network evolve from 2000 to 2015, and which proximities and linkages explain country-pair collaboration?
papers.data: Web of Science country co-authorship data, 2000-2015.
papers.methods: Social network analysis (core-periphery structure, centrality) and Quadratic Assignment Procedure (QAP) regression on country-pair matrices.

The network grew in nodes and ties and shows a core-periphery structure with a more competitive multi-centric core, with the USA as a top-level hub. In the QAP analysis, post-colonial links, a shared English language, economic and science-capability proximity, social proximity and international students are associated with more collaboration. Geographic distance has a negative but statistically insignificant effect.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest network-plus-dyadic-regression analogue in this topic. It already enters a human-mobility dyadic variable (international students) and colonial ties as predictors of country-pair co-authorship. papers.title: Impact of scientific, economic, geopolitical, and cultural factors on international research collaboration
papers.authors: Lei Hou; Yueling Pan; Jonathan J. H. Zhu
papers.research_question: How do scientific size, economic size, geopolitical ties (shared intergovernmental organization memberships) and cultural links (language, religion) shape close collaboration between countries?
papers.data: Country-pair international collaboration data. The data source and years were not confirmed, since only abstract-level material was seen.
papers.methods: Dyadic country-pair analysis of collaboration intensity on scientific, economic, geopolitical and cultural covariates. The exact estimator was not confirmed.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Countries with large and similar scientific and economic sizes are more likely to collaborate closely. Shared memberships in intergovernmental organizations strongly promote close collaboration. Shared language and religion also help.
papers.relevance_to_project: A recent country-pair determinants study that gives a covariate set for the PPML co-authorship baseline (mass terms, size similarity, shared IGOs, language, religion). Migrant stocks and scholarly mobility should be tested as additions to these predictors.

papers.title: Field-normalized citation impact indicators and the choice of an appropriate counting method
papers.authors: Ludo Waltman; Nees Jan van Eck
papers.research_question: Which counting method (full or fractional, and which fractional variant) gives properly field-normalized indicators for countries and organizations?
papers.data: Web of Science publications and citations (CWTS); also arXiv:1501.04431. Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Theoretical argument plus empirical comparison of full counting and several fractional counting variants.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Full counting does not give properly field-normalized results, while fractional counting does. The authors recommend fractional counting for field-normalized studies, especially at country and organization level.
papers.relevance_to_project: Shapes how the OpenAlex co-authorship edges are weighted: full counts of papers per dyad versus fractional/author-share weights. The choice changes gravity estimates and partner distributions, especially for small African systems with very high international co-authorship shares. Both should be run as a robustness check.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: EconPapers RePEc record (J. Informetrics 9(4):872-894) giving DOI 10.1016/j.joi.2015.08.001, and the arXiv preprint 1501.04431.

papers.title: Africa's contribution to the worldwide research literature: New analytical perspectives, trends, and performance indicators
papers.authors: Robert J. W. Tijssen
papers.research_question: How large is Africa's research output and how has it changed (1980-2004) in international and national/regional journals, and what do co-publication patterns show?
papers.data: Research publications by Africa-based authors, 1980-2004, in international journals (Web of Science) and in national and regional journals.
papers.methods: Descriptive scientometric trend and performance indicators, including international co-publication shares.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Africa's share of worldwide science in international journals declined steadily over the period, while international co-publication grew considerably.
papers.relevance_to_project: Historical baseline showing African science becoming more internationally co-authored while its global share shrank. This makes partner choice (former colonial powers, the US, South Africa) central to comparing collaboration partners with migrant destinations.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc page whose URL encodes 10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3 (Scientometrics v71 i2, pp. 303-327) and a link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3 result. papers.title: Neo-colonialism and research collaboration in Central Africa
papers.authors: Nelius Boshoff
papers.research_question: Do Central African research collaborations show neo-colonial ties (dominance of former colonial powers), and what roles do local researchers play?
papers.data: Research papers from Central African countries (bibliometric data), plus a survey of reprint authors of Cameroonian papers.
papers.methods: Bibliometric partner-share analysis combined with an author survey.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. About 80% of the region's papers involve a partner outside Central Africa, and about 35% include a former colonial power. France, the USA, the UK and Germany are the leading partners. Local researchers contribute intellectually, but their most common role is fieldwork.
papers.relevance_to_project: Evidence that colonial history structures African co-authorship partners. It motivates a colonial-tie covariate in the PPML model and a test of whether migrant-destination and collaboration-partner alignment is driven by shared colonial links (as with Francophone Senegal versus Anglophone East and West Africa).
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: Springer article page (link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11192-008-2211-8) citing Scientometrics 81, 413-434 (2009), and the matching IDEAS/RePEc record.

papers.title: International collaboration clusters in Africa
papers.authors: Jonathan Adams; Karen Gurney; Daniel Hook; Loet Leydesdorff
papers.research_question: Is African international research collaboration organized in a uniform global pattern, or in regional clusters shaped by geography, history, culture and language?
papers.data: African country co-authorship data (about 2011 publications, as described in the preprint). The data details were not verified from the full text.
papers.methods: Co-authorship network mapping and clustering (VOSviewer maps).
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. African collaboration is far from universal. It shows layers of internal clusters and external links, explained by regional geography and, more strongly, by history, culture and language rather than global influences. The authors call for analysis of bottom-up human factors to inform policy.
papers.relevance_to_project: Directly about the focus region. It predicts that co-authorship clusters for East African (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda), West African (Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal) and Southern African origins follow linguistic and historical lines. These same factors also shape migration, so they are confounders to control when testing whether migration predicts collaboration.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: Springer page link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11192-013-1060-2 and the arXiv preprint 1301.5159 listing the Scientometrics 98, 547-556 (2014) publication.

papers.title: International collaboration in scientific publishing: the case of West Africa (2001-2010)
papers.authors: Eustache Mêgnigbêto
papers.research_question: Who are West African countries' co-authorship partners, and how much do they collaborate with each other compared with African and non-African countries?
papers.data: Web of Science publications with at least one author affiliated in any of the 15 West African countries, 2001-2010.
papers.methods: Descriptive bibliometric co-authorship partner analysis.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. The main African partners are South Africa, Cameroon, Kenya and Tanzania. The main non-African partners are France, the USA and the UK, which together account for over 63% of papers with a non-West-African address. West African countries collaborate less with each other and with other African and developing countries than with developed countries.
papers.relevance_to_project: Gives expected collaboration-partner profiles for Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal (France/US/UK dominance and weak intra-regional ties) to compare with their UN DESA migrant-destination profiles, which are often more regional (ECOWAS corridors). This is a likely source of misalignment.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc URL encoding 10.1007/s11192-013-0963-2 (Scientometrics v96 i3), the University of Antwerp repository record, and a doi.org/10.1007/S11192-013-0963-2 result.

papers.title: Knowledge production through collaborative research in sub-Saharan Africa: how much do countries contribute to each other's knowledge output and citation impact?
papers.authors: Omwoyo Bosire Onyancha; Jan Resenga Maluleka
papers.research_question: How much do sub-Saharan African countries co-produce knowledge with each other, compared with partners outside the region, and what is the citation impact?
papers.data: Publications and citations of sub-Saharan African countries (bibliometric database). Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Co-authorship (co-production) and citation counts by country pair.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Collaboration among sub-Saharan African countries is minimal and contributes only a small share compared with collaboration with foreign partners. The authors recommend student and staff exchange, regional conferences and research networks.
papers.relevance_to_project: Documents weak intra-SSA co-authorship. Since a large share of SSA migrant stock stays within the region (e.g., Somalia to Kenya/Ethiopia, Uganda to Kenya), this predicts a structural gap between the migration layer and the knowledge layer for the focus origins.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc URL encoding 10.1007/s11192-010-0330-5 (Scientometrics v87 i2) and the Unpaywall/Unisa repository records for the same DOI.

papers.title: Research emphasis and collaboration in Africa
papers.authors: Anastassios Pouris; Yuh-Shan Ho
papers.research_question: Which disciplines does African research emphasize, and what are African collaboration patterns at country and continental level?
papers.data: African publications (bibliometric database). Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Co-authorship analysis at country and continental level, plus disciplinary profiling.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Collaboration rates in Africa are substantially higher than in the rest of the world. Research emphasis leans toward medical and natural-resource disciplines rather than fields supporting knowledge-based economies.
papers.relevance_to_project: The very high international co-authorship share of African output means OpenAlex co-authorship edges for focus origins are dense and partner-heavy. This matters for null-model design and for full versus fractional counting. The medical emphasis suggests field-specific partner structures (e.g., global health funders).
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc URL encoding 10.1007/s11192-013-1156-8 (Scientometrics v98 i3) and the University of Pretoria repository postprint citing doi:10.1007/s11192-013-1156-8.

papers.title: Travel bans and scientific mobility: utility of asymmetry and affinity indexes to inform science policy
papers.authors: Zaida Chinchilla-Rodríguez; Yi Bu; Nicolás Robinson-García; Rodrigo Costas; Cassidy R. Sugimoto
papers.research_question: How are the countries named in the 2017 US travel bans connected to the rest of the world through scientific collaboration and through scholarly mobility, and can asymmetry and affinity indicators compare the two?
papers.data: Bibliometric co-authorship and author-affiliation-based mobility data (CWTS/Web of Science) for the travel-ban countries. Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Asymmetry indexes, the Affinity Index (AFI) and the Probabilistic Affinity Index (PAI), computed separately for collaboration and mobility links and then compared.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. Comparing collaboration and mobility from an affinity perspective reveals mismatches between the two kinds of country linkage. The probabilistic affinity index is highly sensitive and shows that scientific size is limited as a predictor of relationships. The authors propose the approach to inform immigration and science policy.
papers.relevance_to_project: The closest methodological precedent for comparing a mobility layer with a collaboration layer at the country-pair level, including size-adjusted expected-versus-observed (affinity) measures. These are conceptually close to the planned residual analysis. The project extends it by adding general (non-scholarly) migrant stocks from UN DESA and by focusing on Sub-Saharan African origins.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: Springer page link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11192-018-2738-2 and IDEAS/RePEc URL encoding the same DOI (Scientometrics v116 i1), plus the Leiden open-access repository (hdl 1887/67511).

papers.title: Inventor diasporas and the internationalization of technology
papers.authors: Ernest Miguelez
papers.research_question: Do skilled (inventor) diasporas in industrialized countries increase international co-inventorship and other internationalized inventive activity with their developing and emerging origin countries?
papers.data: Patent-based measures of inventor migration (diaspora stocks) and international co-patenting between industrialized countries and developing/emerging economies. Abstract-level only.
papers.methods: Gravity models of internationalized inventive activity between country pairs, with inventor diaspora stocks as the key regressor.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. The link between inventor diasporas and international co-patenting is strong and robust, but weakens as interactions become more formal. The results are not driven by the Chinese and Indian diasporas.
papers.relevance_to_project: The direct methodological template for 'gravity of knowledge collaboration with and without migrant stocks', applied to patents rather than papers. It shows that skilled diaspora stocks predict co-production. The project tests whether general UN DESA migrant stocks (mostly not scholars) do the same for scientific co-authorship once scholarly mobility is controlled.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: EconPapers RePEc record (World Bank Economic Review 32(1):41-63), with the HAL (hal-03125171) and Bordeaux repository records reporting DOI 10.1093/wber/lhw013. Earlier version: World Bank Policy Research WP 7619 (2016).

papers.title: An analysis of the suitability of OpenAlex for bibliometric analyses
papers.authors: Juan Pablo Alperin; Jason Portenoy; Kyle Demes; Vincent Larivière; Stefanie Haustein
papers.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.17663 (cs.DL); no journal version found as of search
papers.research_question: Can OpenAlex replace Scopus for bibliometric analyses, and how do coverage and metadata compare?
papers.data: OpenAlex and Scopus records (secondary summaries mention a late-2023 OpenAlex snapshot). The study was done in collaboration with the OpenAlex team.
papers.methods: Comparison of coverage and metadata between OpenAlex and Scopus across several dimensions, including country-level rank correlations.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. OpenAlex is a superset of Scopus and can be a reliable alternative for some analyses, particularly at the country level, but metadata accuracy and completeness issues remain. A substantial share of OpenAlex works lack affiliation/country information or references (from secondary summaries).
papers.relevance_to_project: Supports country-level OpenAlex co-authorship networks while flagging missing affiliations. Missing affiliations would bias co-authorship edges for origins with weaker metadata (likely including several SSA countries). The project should report the share of works with missing country codes per origin.
papers.verification_source: WebSearch results: arXiv listing arxiv.org/abs/2404.17663 (submitted 26 Apr 2024), with the search result reporting arXiv DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2404.17663. No journal DOI found.

papers.title: Coverage and metadata availability of African publications in OpenAlex: A comparative analysis (PDF title: 'Coverage and metadata completeness and accuracy of African research publications in OpenAlex: A comparative analysis')
papers.authors: Patricia Alonso-Álvarez; Nees Jan van Eck
papers.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2409.01120 (cs.DL); no journal version found as of search
papers.research_question: How do OpenAlex, Scopus, Web of Science and African Journals Online (AJOL) compare in their coverage and metadata for publications in African-based journals?
papers.data: Publications in African-based academic journals, 1996-2022, matched across OpenAlex, Scopus, WoS and AJOL by exact DOI match.
papers.methods: Coverage overlap comparison and metadata-availability comparison (authors, affiliations, references, funders) across databases.
papers.findings: Abstract-level only. OpenAlex has the most extensive coverage of these African publications. It has high coverage of publication and author metadata but performs worse on affiliations, references and funder information. Metadata availability is better for publications also indexed in Scopus or WoS.
papers.relevance_to_project: The most directly relevant evidence on OpenAlex quality for African research. Broad coverage helps the co-authorship layer, but weak affiliation metadata can drop or misassign country links for SSA origins. Caveat: the sample is African-based journals, not all African-authored work.
papers.verification_source: Title, authors, year and arXiv ID confirmed from arXiv listing results (arxiv.org/abs/2409.01120, submitted 2 Sep 2024). No DOI was seen in any source, so doi is null. The title differs between the arXiv abstract page and the PDF.

established: International co-authorship has grown rapidly and is widely modeled as a self-organizing country network with preferential attachment and a core-periphery structure (Wagner & Leydesdorff 2005, doi 10.1016/j.respol.2005.08.002; Wagner, Park & Leydesdorff 2015, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0131816; also Leydesdorff & Wagner 2008, J. Informetrics 2(4):317-325, doi 10.1016/j.joi.2008.07.003, on a core group of 14 most cooperative countries, verified via EconPapers). Null models should preserve degree/strength, because hub dominance is expected.
Bilateral co-authorship links are not always symmetric, and the citation benefit of international co-authorship differs by country and field (Glänzel 2001, doi 10.1023/A:1010512628145).

Count-based gravity models of co-publications are standard: distance and borders reduce collaboration, and distance sensitivity has not declined over time even as border effects fall (Hoekman, Frenken & Tijssen 2010, doi 10.1016/j.respol.2010.01.012). Several proximities (geographic, cognitive, institutional, social, economic) jointly predict co-authorship (Fernández, Ferrándiz & León 2016, doi 10.1007/s11192-015-1819-8; also Ponds, van Oort & Frenken 2007, Papers in Regional Science 86(3):423-443, doi 10.1111/j.1435-5957.2007.00126.x).

At the country-pair level, scientific and economic size and size similarity, shared intergovernmental memberships, shared language/religion, post-colonial ties and international student flows are associated with more co-authorship (Hou, Pan & Zhu 2021, doi 10.1016/j.joi.2021.101194; Gui, Liu & Du 2019, doi 10.1016/j.geoforum.2019.06.017). Colonial history and language are therefore shared confounders of the migration and knowledge layers.

Counting method matters: full counting does not produce properly field-normalized indicators, so fractional counting is recommended at country level (Waltman & van Eck 2015, doi 10.1016/j.joi.2015.08.001). Fractional counting lowers relative indicators most for countries with the highest international co-authorship shares (Aksnes, Schneider & Gunnarsson 2012, J. Informetrics 6(1):36-43, doi 10.1016/j.joi.2011.08.002, verified via EconPapers). This bears directly on small African systems.

African research is highly internationally co-authored, with collaboration rates above the world average (Pouris & Ho 2014, doi 10.1007/s11192-013-1156-8). International co-publication grew while Africa's share of world output declined (Tijssen 2007, doi 10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3). Output has grown quickly since about 2004 (Confraria & Godinho 2015, Scientometrics 102(2):1241-1268, doi 10.1007/s11192-014-1463-8, verified via IDEAS).

African co-authorship partners are dominated by former colonial powers and the US (France, USA, UK, Germany in Central Africa: Boshoff 2009, doi 10.1007/s11192-008-2211-8; France, USA, UK account for more than 63% of extra-regional West African co-papers: Mêgnigbêto 2013, doi 10.1007/s11192-013-0963-2). Intra-SSA collaboration is weak (Onyancha & Maluleka 2011, doi 10.1007/s11192-010-0330-5; see also Toivanen & Ponomariov 2011, Scientometrics 88(2):471-493, doi 10.1007/s11192-011-0390-1, verified via Springer/IDEAS). Collaboration clusters follow geography, history, culture and language (Adams, Gurney, Hook & Leydesdorff 2014, doi 10.1007/s11192-013-1060-2).

Skilled-diaspora stocks predict international co-invention in gravity models (Miguelez 2018, doi 10.1093/wber/lhw013). Migrant and returnee scientists have larger international networks and often collaborate with their origin country (Scellato, Franzoni & Stephan 2015, Research Policy 44(1):108-120, doi 10.1016/j.respol.2014.07.014, verified via EconPapers; survey-based, 16 destination countries).
Collaboration and scholarly mobility linkages between countries can diverge once size is accounted for (affinity indexes; Chinchilla-Rodríguez et al. 2018, doi 10.1007/s11192-018-2738-2).

OpenAlex has broader coverage than Scopus/WoS and is considered usable for country-level analyses, but affiliation/country, reference and funder metadata are weaker (Alperin et al. 2024, arXiv:2404.17663; Alonso-Álvarez & van Eck 2024, arXiv:2409.01120, for African-based journals). OpenAlex reference coverage is comparable to WoS/Scopus on the shared set of publications (Culbert et al. 2025, Scientometrics 130(4):2475-2492, doi 10.1007/s11192-025-05293-3, verified via IDEAS). OpenAlex language coverage is more balanced than WoS, but its language metadata are often inaccurate (Céspedes et al. 2025, JASIST 76(6):884-895, doi 10.1002/asi.24979, verified via EconPapers RePEc:bla:jinfst:v:76:y:2025:i:6:p:884-895).
unresolved: No study was found that compares, for the same origin countries, the destination distribution of general (UN DESA) migrant stocks with both the co-authorship-partner distribution and the bibliometric scholarly mobility flows. Existing work pairs mobility with collaboration (Chinchilla-Rodríguez et al. 2018) or diaspora with co-patenting (Miguelez 2018), but not all three layers, and not for Sub-Saharan African origins.

Whether general migrant stocks, which for SSA origins are largely intra-regional and refugee-heavy (e.g., Somalia, South Sudan to neighbours), carry any information about co-authorship once scholarly mobility, colonial ties, language and mass terms are controlled. The diaspora-gravity evidence concerns skilled/inventor diasporas only.

No recent all-discipline, OpenAlex-based study of sub-Saharan African international co-authorship patterns (2024-2025) was found in this search. The search surfaced only field-specific work, such as a 2026 education-research study by van Schalkwyk, González-Salmón and Robinson-García (not verified in detail). Older SSA collaboration studies rely on WoS/Scopus.

The size of OpenAlex affiliation/country-metadata gaps for the specific focus countries (Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, South Africa) is not quantified in the literature found. Alonso-Álvarez & van Eck cover African-based journals only, and Alperin et al. report global country-level agreement.

The best counting scheme for dyadic gravity models of co-authorship (full paper counts per dyad, fractional author shares, or binary presence) is not settled for PPML. Waltman & van Eck and Aksnes et al. address citation indicators, not dyadic flow models.

Data sources and estimators for Hou, Pan & Zhu (2021) and the full methods of Gui, Liu & Du (2019) were read only at abstract level and should be checked in the full text before being cited for methodological detail.

Access limits: api.crossref.org and publisher sites (e.g., journals.plos.org) were unreachable via WebFetch in this session. All DOI verification relied on WebSearch result pages (IDEAS/RePEc, EconPapers, Springer link pages, PMC, institutional repositories, arXiv). Findings are abstract-level paraphrases. The DOI for Alonso-Álvarez & van Eck (arXiv:2409.01120) was not seen and is left null.
sweep.closest_prior_work_to_our_contribution: The closest prior work is Chinchilla-Rodríguez, Bu, Robinson-García, Costas & Sugimoto (2018, Scientometrics 116(1):569-590, doi 10.1007/s11192-018-2738-2). It compares scientific collaboration and bibliometric scholarly mobility at the country level for the 2017 US travel-ban countries. It uses size-adjusted affinity indexes (observed versus expected) and finds mismatches between the two layers, which is conceptually very close to the project's per-origin alignment and residual analysis. On the regression side, Miguelez (2018, World Bank Economic Review 32(1):41-63, doi 10.1093/wber/lhw013) estimates gravity models of international co-patenting with inventor-diaspora stocks and finds strong, robust diaspora effects. That is the direct template for 'PPML with and without migrant stocks', applied to patents rather than papers. Gui, Liu & Du (2019, Geoforum, doi 10.1016/j.geoforum.2019.06.017) add international student flows and colonial ties to a country-pair (QAP) model of co-authorship. The project's contribution relative to these: (a) a three-layer comparison of general UN DESA migrant stocks, Akbaritabar et al. scholarly mobility and OpenAlex co-authorship; (b) a focus on Sub-Saharan African origins, where the African-collaboration literature (Boshoff 2009; Mêgnigbêto 2013; Onyancha & Maluleka 2011; Adams et al. 2014) predicts partners dominated by former colonial powers and the US with weak intra-regional ties, while migration is often intra-regional; (c) explicit per-origin alignment metrics plus multilayer topology comparison with degree/strength-preserving nulls, which none of these prior studies combine.

established: Gravity equations should be estimated in levels by PPML, not OLS on logs. Under heteroskedasticity, log-linearized OLS gives inconsistent elasticities and in trade applications overstates distance effects (Santos Silva & Tenreyro 2006, abstract-level).

PPML with several high-dimensional fixed effects (origin, destination, year) is routine with ppmlhdfe, which also detects separation and non-existence of estimates (Correia, Guimaraes & Zylkin 2020). This matters for sparse SSA dyads with many zeros.

A theory-consistent gravity specification needs origin and destination fixed effects (multilateral resistance), and using several estimators as a toolkit is recommended (Head & Mayer 2014, abstract-level).

A gravity model can reproduce weighted network structure well while failing to predict which links exist and missing clustering (Duenas & Fagiolo 2013). Binary and weighted fit should be evaluated separately.

Gravity residual networks can have very different, more complex topology than the raw network. Small countries show up as local hubs once size and distance are removed (Fagiolo 2010). This supports a residual-network analysis.

In weighted networks, the degree sequence carries information the strength sequence does not. Nulls should therefore constrain both, e.g. the enhanced configuration model (Mastrandrea et al. 2014), and analytical maximum-entropy methods give null expectations and variances without sampling (Squartini & Garlaschelli 2011).

Maximum-entropy null parameters can be tied to economic mass variables such as GDP. Binary structure is inferable from such fitness variables, but weighted structure needs binary information (Almog, Squartini & Garlaschelli 2015).

The disparity filter extracts backbones from local significance of edge weights relative to each node's strength, keeping links at all scales instead of using a global threshold (Serrano, Boguna & Vespignani 2009).

Multiplex structure can be summarized by edge overlap: pairwise o_ij is the number of layers linking i and j, and the multiplex-level overlap runs from 1/M (no shared edges) to 1 (identical layers), alongside cross-layer degree correlations and interlayer clustering (Battiston, Nicosia & Latora 2014).

Layer redundancy can be tested formally. Structural reducibility merges layers using von Neumann entropy and Jensen-Shannon distances, and in real systems up to 75% of layers can be uninformative (De Domenico et al. 2015).
The Jensen-Shannon divergence is bounded and needs no absolute continuity, so it suits comparing distributions with non-overlapping support (Lin 1991).

Dyadic regressions need dependence-robust inference: multiway clustering for non-nested dimensions (Cameron, Gelbach & Miller 2011), and dyad-robust variance that allows correlation between any dyads sharing a member (Aronow, Samii & Assenova 2015).

Global bilateral migrant stocks are built from harmonized destination censuses and registers with imputation. South-south migration was about half of global migration in 2000 (Ozden et al. 2011). Stocks differ from flows, and flows can be estimated from stock changes, with closed demographic accounting performing best (Abel & Cohen 2019).

CEPII GeoDist provides population-weighted bilateral distances and dyadic dummies (contiguity, common language, colonial ties) for 225 countries and is the standard covariate source for gravity models (Mayer & Zignago 2011).

# OpenAlex API (late 2026): documentation review, blocked

## Access status: read this first

**I could not read any current OpenAlex documentation, so nothing below is verified for late 2026.**

- **WebSearch:** the first call came back "budget used up (200 calls per turn, shared by all agents)".
- **WebFetch:** `docs.openalex.org` and `developers.openalex.org` both failed with `ENOTFOUND`. The tool says this means the host is outside the session's allowed network domains, or does not exist. Its instructions say to stop trying other hosts after that, so I did not try `help.openalex.org`, the blog or GitHub pages.
- **GitHub MCP:** `ourresearch/openalex-docs` was refused. This session only allows `dmzysz7ck6-del/net`.
- **The API itself:** `api.openalex.org` is also blocked at the container's egress, per `/home/user/Net/migration-knowledge/research/progress.md`.

So every item below is my background knowledge, with a training cutoff of June 2026, plus a confidence level and a check you can run at no cost. **No source URL is given, because I saw none.** Nothing here should be cited in the paper until it is checked.

**To unblock:** allow `docs.openalex.org`, `developers.openalex.org`, `help.openalex.org`, `api.openalex.org` and `openalex.s3.amazonaws.com` (the free snapshot) in the session's network settings. Or send a follow-up message, so the search budget resets, and re-run this step.

## Facts (all UNVERIFIED; confidence H/M/L)

### 1. Authentication, limits and cost
- **F1 (H for the past, L for now).** From 2022 to 2024 no key was needed. Limits were 100,000 calls per day and 10 requests per second. Adding `mailto=` or an email in the User-Agent put you in the "polite pool".
- **F2 (L on details).** In 2025–26 OpenAlex moved to API keys and usage-based pricing. Different request types cost different amounts: single-record lookups, list/filter, search, and full-text downloads. There is a free daily allowance and paid usage above it. I don't reliably remember:
  - whether a key is now mandatory;
  - the size of the free allowance;
  - whether a `group_by` call costs the same as a list call.
- **F3 (M).** A paid "Premium" tier for higher limits existed earlier.
- **Check / zero-cost rule:**
  - Read the authentication and rate-limit page.
  - Send one call with `api_key` and one without, and compare the response headers (any rate-limit or credit headers) and the `meta` block.
  - Never add a payment method to the account.
  - Make the client stop on HTTP 402 or 429 instead of retrying.

### 2. Works fields
- **`authorships[].countries` (M).** A list of ISO-2 codes per author. It comes from the matched institutions. My recollection is that it is also filled from raw affiliation strings when no institution could be matched.
- **`authorships[].institutions[].country_code` (H).** The country of the matched (ROR-linked) institution.
- **`authorships[].raw_affiliation_strings` and `authorships[].affiliations[]` (M-H).** The raw strings, plus the institution IDs each string was matched to.
- **`countries_distinct_count` and `institutions_distinct_count` (H that they exist; L-M on how they are computed).** Distinct countries or institutions across all authorships. It is unclear whether the country count is built from `authorships.countries` or only from institution country codes. This matters for the k-bin method below.
- **`type` (M-H).** Values since 2023:
  - article, book-chapter, dataset, preprint, dissertation, book, review, paratext, libguides, letter;
  - other, reference-entry, report, editorial, peer-review, erratum, standard, grant, supplementary-material, retraction.

  OpenAlex assigns review, paratext, letter, editorial and erratum with its own rules. `type_crossref` keeps the Crossref type, such as journal-article.
- **`primary_location.source.type` (M).** journal, repository, conference, ebook platform, book series, metadata, other.
- **Other fields (M-H).** `is_retracted` and `is_paratext` are booleans and `publication_year` is an integer. `has_fulltext` means OpenAlex holds the full text; it says nothing about affiliations. `indexed_in` lists sources such as crossref, pubmed, doaj and arxiv.
- **Walden, the 2025 rewrite (L).** I recall it reprocessed works and added a large batch of non-Crossref records. I believe they are flagged `is_xpac` and excluded by default. Type assignment and affiliation matching may also have changed.
  - **Check:** run `group_by=type` and `group_by=countries_distinct_count` for a fixed filter, compare against older figures, and record the data date in provenance.

### 3. Filter syntax
- **Basics (H).**
  - A comma means AND across filters.
  - `|` means OR within one filter, e.g. `authorships.countries:KE|UG`. There is a cap on the number of OR values; I recall 50, confidence L.
  - A leading `!` negates, e.g. `type:!paratext`.
  - `>` and `<` work on numbers, e.g. `countries_distinct_count:>1`.
  - A hyphen gives a range, e.g. `publication_year:2015-2019`.
  - `+` may mean AND within one filter (L-M).
- **Repeating a filter (M-H).** `authorships.countries:KE,authorships.countries:US` returns works that include both KE and US. This was documented for `institutions.country_code`.
  - **Check:** its count should equal the US bucket of `group_by=authorships.countries` run under the filter `authorships.countries:KE`.
- **Ranges on the country count (M).** `countries_distinct_count:>1,countries_distinct_count:<5` should give works with 2 to 4 countries.

### 4. group_by
- **Format (H).** The request is `group_by=<field>`. The response has a `group_by` list of `{key, key_display_name, count}` entries and `meta.groups_count`.
- **Groupable fields (M / L-M).** `authorships.countries` can be grouped (M). Whether `countries_distinct_count` can be is L-M, and the existing code assumes it can.
- **Number of groups (M / L-M).** Historically at most 200 groups per page (M). Cursor paging for `group_by`, via `meta.next_cursor`, is L-M. There are only about 250 countries, so this means at most 2 pages.
- **Unknown group (L-M).** Works with no value can appear under the key `unknown`. A suffix such as `:include_unknown` may control this.
- **Exact or approximate counts (L).** I'm not sure whether the counts are exact. The backend is Elasticsearch, whose grouped counts can be approximate. The sum checks below will show whether they are.

### 5. Paging
- **(H)** `per_page` runs from 1 to 200 (default 25).
- **(H)** `page=N` only reaches the first 10,000 results. For anything deeper, use `cursor=*` and follow `meta.next_cursor` until it is null.
- **(M)** `select=` takes top-level fields only, with no nested selection. I believe it can't be combined with `group_by` (L).

### 6. Data-quality caveats
These are leads to confirm. The papers are named from memory: DOIs are null and none are verified.
- **Missing institutions or affiliations.** Many authorships have no institution, especially for older works and some publishers. Those works get k = 0 or too small a k. Lead: Zhang et al., *Scientometrics* 2024, "Missing institutions in OpenAlex…".
- **Country derived from affiliation strings can be wrong.** Likely confusions: Niger vs Nigeria, Guinea vs Guinea-Bissau vs Equatorial Guinea, the two Congos, and the US state of Georgia vs the country.
- **Document types differ from WoS and Scopus.** Some editorial items are labelled article, and reviews are detected differently. Lead: Haupka et al., arXiv 2024.
- **Wider coverage.** OpenAlex covers more Global South and non-English journals than WoS or Scopus. Leads: Alperin et al., arXiv 2024; Céspedes et al., *JASIST* 2025. One consequence: African output will look larger in OpenAlex than in the Scopus-based Akbaritabar et al. mobility data, which will distort the layer comparison.
- **Counts change over time.** Monthly updates and the Walden reprocessing shift numbers. Record the date of every extraction.
- **Mega-collaborations.** Papers with 20+ countries inflate full counts. Fractional counting and the existing threshold of 20 (`mega_country_threshold`) address this.

## Recommended query strategy

**Base filter F:** `type:article,primary_location.source.type:journal,is_retracted:false,is_paratext:false,publication_year:Y1-Y2`. This matches `config/pipeline.yaml`. As a sensitivity check, also run with `type_crossref:journal-article` and with reviews included.

**(c) Article output per country-year.** One call per year covers every country: `group_by=authorships.countries` with F and `publication_year:y`. Also run `group_by=countries_distinct_count` per year to track the share of works with no country (k = 0 or unknown). This is about 1–2 calls per year, instead of one per country.

**(a) and (b) for a focal country X and window w:**
1. Run `group_by=countries_distinct_count` with F and `authorships.countries:X`. This gives N_k(X), the number of X's works with exactly k countries.
2. For each k ≥ 2 with N_k > 0 and k ≤ K* (about 25), run `group_by=authorships.countries` with F, `authorships.countries:X` and `countries_distinct_count:k`. This gives n_k(X,Y) for every partner Y. Drop Y = X.
3. For the tail (k > K*), either run per-k calls only for the k values that actually occur, or download those works once per window for all countries together. For the download, use cursor paging with `select=id,countries_distinct_count,authorships` and compute the weights exactly.
4. Full count: full(X,Y) = Σ_k n_k(X,Y).
5. Fractional count: frac(X,Y) = Σ_k n_k(X,Y) · 2/(k(k−1)). Each work then carries a total weight of 1 across its pairs.

**Cost.** Each (X, window) needs about 1 + (number of k values present) calls. For roughly 200 focal countries, 3 windows and about 20 k values on average, that is about 12,000 calls; year by year it is about 60,000. The gravity models need every dyad, so every country has to be queried as X. If F2 turns out to make that many calls cost money, use the free S3 snapshot instead. It allows exact local computation, including the R8 inter-author variant; its terms are also unverified.

**Free consistency checks (no extra calls):**
- **Sum check.** Σ_Y n_k(X,Y), including Y = X, should equal k·N_k(X). If it doesn't, one of three things is true:
  - the counts are approximate;
  - groups were cut off;
  - `countries_distinct_count` is built from a different country source than `authorships.countries`.
- **Symmetry.** X's query and Y's query should give the same n_k(X,Y). `aggregate_k_table` already checks this.
- **Totals.** Σ_k N_k(X) plus the unknown or k = 0 group should equal the plain count for F with `authorships.countries:X`.
- **Spot check.** For about 20 pairs, the count for `authorships.countries:X,authorships.countries:Y,countries_distinct_count:>1` should equal full(X,Y).

**Problems in the existing code (`/home/user/Net/migration-knowledge/src/acquisition/openalex.py`):**
- `int(str(g["key"]).rsplit("/",1)[-1])` will crash if the API returns an `unknown` key. This affects `country_k_table`, `country_output` and `coverage`.
- `group_by()` should assert that `len(groups) == meta.groups_count`. Otherwise it can silently keep only the first 200 groups if cursor paging isn't supported for `group_by`.
- `cleaning/openalex.py::work_countries` sets k from the union of `authorships.countries` and `institutions[].country_code`. The API's k bins may use a different definition, so the work-level validation should compute k both ways.

**Next step:** once the hosts are allowed, re-run this step to replace the confidence labels with cited facts. Everything in Facts 1–5, and the existence of each paper in 6, can be checked from the documentation pages or with one or two zero-cost API calls each.
